Collaboration

How this developer ships and reviews work. Volume and cadence are context only — no single number captures the full picture. This is not a quality score.

Review > PR ratio. Reviewing significantly more than you ship is characteristic of a tech lead or staff engineer whose primary leverage is raising the team’s quality bar, not personal output. This pattern often signals mentorship load and design-review involvement that don’t show up in PR counts.

Pull requests

47authored

A high volume of merged pull requests indicates sustained, steady contribution across the coverage window.

Limit: volume alone says nothing about the size or quality of the work. A developer who ships many small, well-scoped changes and one who ships a single multi-thousand-line PR both show up here as a count. Use this number as orientation, not as a measure of output.

Pull request size

Based on the 42 merged pull requests with diff data. Research recommends PRs of roughly 200–400 changed lines; review quality degrades sharply past about 1,000 lines. Small-PR discipline is one of the strongest predictors of review thoroughness and team velocity.

256median lines per PR
8median files per PR
76%PRs ≤ 400 lines

Roughly half of pull requests fall within the recommended size range. The other half may benefit from smaller, more focused scoping.

Limit: line counts are not a proxy for code quality. A single-line change to a critical config file may warrant more scrutiny than a hundred lines of well-isolated refactoring. Use this data as one signal among many.

Reviews given

Typical range: 20–40% (Code Climate Velocity Report, 2024). Typical ranges vary by team size and workflow.

A review is a formal platform review submission — approve or request changes — on a teammate’s pull request. Standalone inline comments left without submitting a review are counted separately under Review comments, not here. Deep review % (shown in the summary strip) is the share of reviews where you left three or more inline comments — a rough proxy for depth of engagement.

63total reviews
51approvals
12changes requested

This developer is a very active reviewer, investing significant time in teammates’ work.

Limit: review counts do not capture review depth — a one-word “LGTM” and a detailed structural critique look identical here. The changes-requested count is a rough proxy for engagement, not a quality judgement.

Review comments

Written: inline diff comments you left on other people’s pull requests. Received: inline diff comments others left on your pull requests. Standalone top-level PR comments (not attached to a diff line) are not counted.

124written
89received

Comment counts show the texture of the code-review dialogue: how much inline feedback this developer gives and receives. A higher written count alongside a higher received count often signals active mutual engagement.

Giving more than receiving. Writing more review comments than you receive typically signals that you are operating as a reviewer and mentor, not just a recipient of feedback. Evaluators often read this as a sign of senior engagement and investment in team quality.

Limit: comment counts are extremely noisy. A single heated thread can inflate the number; a highly skilled reviewer who spots the root issue in one sentence will show a low count. Treat this as a rough signal only.

Time to merge

Typical range: 24–72 h (DORA 2024 State of DevOps Report, 2024). Typical ranges vary by team size and workflow.

18.5hmedian
42merged PRs

Pull requests merged quickly on the median, suggesting lightweight scoping, an active review culture, or both.

Limit: this measures elapsed wall-clock time, not working time. Weekend drafts, long-running feature branches opened early, or approval-gate automation all inflate the number without indicating a problem.

Time to first review

Typical range: 7–12 h (LinearB 2025 Benchmark Report, 2025). Typical ranges vary by team size and workflow.

5.2hmedian
40PRs reviewed

How long, on the median, before a teammate picked up this developer’s pull request and left a first review. Short times suggest an attentive team or proactive review culture; longer times can simply reflect cross-timezone work or a small team.

Limit: PRs that were never reviewed are excluded from this calculation. If many PRs go unreviewed, the median understates the typical wait.

Rework rate

Typical range: 15–40% (Springer EMSE, 2019). Typical ranges vary by team size and workflow.

26%of reviewed PRs
11 of 42reviewed

The share of this developer’s reviewed pull requests where at least one reviewer requested changes before approval. A moderate rework rate is common and healthy: it shows that reviewers are engaged and that the author responds to feedback.

Limit: some rework is normal and desirable — it means the review process is working. This metric cannot distinguish between a developer who iterates quickly on feedback and one who struggles. The denominator is reviewed PRs only; unreviewed PRs are excluded.

Tech stack fingerprint

Activity cadence

Volume and cadence are context only — they say nothing about quality. No score is derived from this data.

An active day is any calendar day on which you opened a pull request, submitted a formal review (approve or request changes), or wrote an inline review comment on someone else’s PR. Commits, merges, issue comments, and activity received on your own PRs are not counted. Contributions is the total number of those individual events across the window.
